name: DPAGT1-CDG (congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ij)

clinicalPearls: DPAGT1 encodes the enzyme catalysing the first committed and rate-limiting step of N-linked glycosylation, transferring N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate from UDP-GlcNAc onto dolichol phosphate on the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum, so its deficiency produces a type I (assembly) CDG.
Two contrasting phenotypes exist: a severe multisystem disorder with epileptic encephalopathy, and a much milder limb-girdle congenital myasthenic syndrome.
The severe CDG-Ij form features profound developmental delay, intractable seizures, microcephaly, marked hypotonia, feeding difficulty and often cataract.

The myasthenic form presents with fatigable, predominantly limb-girdle weakness with relative sparing of ocular and facial muscles, reflecting impaired glycosylation and clustering of the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction.
Muscle biopsy in the myasthenic phenotype characteristically shows tubular aggregates.
The myasthenic weakness typically responds well to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, in contrast to the largely supportive management of the encephalopathic form.
Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type 1 pattern in the multisystem form, but may be subtle or near-normal in the myasthenic phenotype, so molecular confirmation is essential.
Because glycosylation is a shared final pathway, clinical overlap with other type I CDGs means DPAGT1 cannot be distinguished from PMM2 or ALG defects on phenotype alone.
reference.pathophysiology: DPAGT1 (dolichyl-phosphate N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase) initiates assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide in the endoplasmic reticulum by transferring N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphate from UDP-GlcNAc onto the lipid carrier dolichol phosphate to generate GlcNAc-pyrophosphate-dolichol. This is the first and rate-limiting committed step of N-glycan synthesis, so loss of function truncates or abolishes the lipid-linked precursor and reduces occupancy of N-glycosylation sites (hypoglycosylation) across many glycoproteins. Because assembly and clustering of the acetylcholine receptor depend on adequate N-glycosylation, a partial deficiency can manifest selectively as a congenital myasthenic syndrome, whereas more severe loss of function disrupts maturation of glycoproteins throughout the body and produces the multisystem encephalopathic phenotype. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: PMM2-CDG and other type I congenital disorders of glycosylation
ALG-family CDGs (for example ALG1, ALG2, ALG13)
Other congenital myasthenic syndromes (GFPT1, RAPSN, CHRNE, CHAT)
Spinal muscular atrophy and other early hypotonia syndromes (for the myasthenic phenotype)
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing or glycoform analysis (type 1 pattern)
DPAGT1 molecular genetic testing via a targeted CDG or congenital myasthenic syndrome panel or exome sequencing
Repetitive nerve stimulation and single-fibre electromyography (decrement in the myasthenic form)
Muscle biopsy looking for tubular aggregates
Electroencephalography and neuroimaging in the encephalopathic phenotype
Lipid-linked oligosaccharide analysis in cultured fibroblasts (specialist laboratory)
redFlags: Intractable neonatal or infantile seizures with developmental regression
Rapidly progressive respiratory or bulbar weakness suggesting myasthenic crisis
Marked worsening of weakness during intercurrent fever or infection in the myasthenic form
reference.prognosis: The severe multisystem form carries high morbidity with profound disability and early mortality, whereas the limb-girdle myasthenic phenotype is compatible with prolonged survival and often improves substantially with acetylcholinesterase inhibitor therapy.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal or borderline transferrin study excludes CDG, as glycosylation abnormalities can be subtle in the myasthenic phenotype
Misdiagnosing the myasthenic form as seronegative autoimmune myasthenia gravis and giving immunosuppression instead of cholinesterase inhibitors
Overlooking a treatable myasthenic component in a child labelled as having a limb-girdle myopathy
Using neuromuscular blocking or weakness-provoking agents without recognising the underlying neuromuscular junction vulnerability
references: Congenital disorders of glycosylation review literature
management: In the limb-girdle congenital myasthenic phenotype, acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as pyridostigmine are the mainstay and typically produce substantial improvement in fatigable weakness
Adjunctive agents used in congenital myasthenic syndromes, such as salbutamol or ephedrine, may be added where the anticholinesterase response is incomplete

The severe encephalopathic form has no specific therapy and is managed supportively, with antiseizure medication for the intractable seizures and nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding for feeding difficulty
Provide developmental therapies (physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy) and management of hypotonia
Arrange ophthalmological review for cataract, with surgical correction as required
Coordinate care through metabolic medicine and neurology, monitoring seizures and neurodevelopmental progress
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with carrier testing and family screening
